summary: Defines how the standard kinds of Directory attribute values, such as text strings and addresses, are written out as strings for LDAP. It also sets the requirements that any such encoding rules must meet. It was replaced by RFC 1778.

eli5.summary: When you fill out a form, each box expects its answer written a certain way. This memo says how each kind of answer should be written down for a directory.

questions: how are directory attributes encoded as strings
how are ldap attributes encoded as strings
subtitle: How Directory attribute values are encoded as strings for LDAP protocol use

tldr.problem: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) requires that all attribute values in directory messages be octet strings, but the X.500 directory defines many different types of values—text, numbers, booleans, addresses, and more—each with its own representation rules.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies encoding rules that convert each standard attribute syntax type into a string form suitable for transmission and display, ensuring that attributes can be read, compared, and displayed correctly across different implementations.
tldr.outcome: Directory clients and servers could reliably exchange directory data in LDAP format, knowing exactly how to encode and decode every standard attribute type, although this RFC was later updated by RFC 1778.

today: RFC 1488 defined the encoding rules for standard X.500 attribute syntaxes in LDAP. It has been updated by RFC 1778, which provides refined definitions. LDAP has become the standard directory access protocol, and these encoding rules remain fundamental to how directory information is transmitted and displayed.

sections.title: Encoding Directory Attributes for LDAP
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is a protocol for accessing directory information—like email addresses, phone numbers, and organization details—stored in an X.500 directory. LDAP messages contain attribute values, but the protocol requires these values to be transmitted as octet strings (bytes). However, the X.500 directory standard defines many different types of attribute values, each with its own structure and rules.

The RFC solves this mismatch by defining how each standard attribute syntax is encoded into a string form. These encoding rules must be reversible (so you can decode the string back to the original value) and should be human-readable to the greatest extent possible. This allows LDAP clients and servers to exchange complex directory data while respecting the semantics of each attribute type.
sections.eli5: When you fill out a form on paper, each box has a different format: a phone number looks like 555-1234, a date looks like March 15, and a name looks like 'Smith, John'. LDAP needs to know how to write all these different kinds of information as text strings.

sections.title: Encoding Simple String Attributes
sections.content:
The RFC defines several simple string attribute types. Case Ignore String attributes are encoded as the string value itself, without special handling. Case Exact String attributes are also encoded as-is, preserving capitalization. Printable String attributes contain only printable ASCII characters—letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation—and are encoded directly. Numeric String attributes contain only digits and are encoded as a digit string.

Octet String attributes contain arbitrary binary data and are encoded as the raw string. IA5 String (IA5 = International Alphabet 5) attributes contain any ASCII character and are encoded as-is. T.61 String attributes use the T.61 character set and are encoded as the string value. For all these types, the rule is straightforward: the encoded form is the string itself, making these attributes easy to read and compare in LDAP output.
sections.eli5: For most kinds of text, you just write it down exactly as it is. A name stays 'Alice', a number stays '12345', and a message stays as written.

sections.title: Encoding Complex Attribute Types
sections.content:
Some attribute types are more complex. Case Ignore List and Case Exact List attributes contain multiple string values separated by the dollar sign character ($). For example, a case-ignore list might be encoded as value1$value2$value3. Distinguished Name attributes identify entries in the directory tree and are encoded according to X.500 DN (Distinguished Name) representation rules, which use a hierarchical comma-separated format like cn=Alice,ou=People,o=Example.

Boolean attributes have only two values and are encoded as the strings TRUE or FALSE. Integer attributes are encoded as the decimal representation of their numeric value. Object Identifier attributes are encoded using either symbolic names (if known) or numeric OID notation, preferring symbolic names whenever possible. This allows an OID like 2.5.4.10 (organization name) to be written as organizationName for readability.
sections.eli5: Lists use a separator (a dollar sign) between items. Names follow a tree format. True and false get spelled out. Numbers are written as digits. And long technical codes can use friendly names if available.

sections.title: Encoding Specialized Attribute Syntaxes
sections.content:
The RFC defines encoding rules for several specialized attribute syntaxes that are common in X.500 directories. Telephone Number attributes are encoded as printable strings. Telex Number attributes have three parts—the number, the country code, and the answerback code—separated by dollar signs in the format number$country$answerback. Teletex Terminal Identifier attributes are encoded as one or more printable string parts separated by dollar signs.

Facsimile Telephone Number attributes contain a phone number optionally followed by fax parameters like resolution and paper size, also separated by dollar signs. Presentation Address attributes are encoded according to X.500 presentation address conventions. These specialized types allow LDAP directories to store and transmit diverse types of contact and technical information while maintaining consistent encoding rules across different LDAP implementations.
sections.eli5: Phone numbers, fax parameters, and specialized codes each have their own format, but they all use printable characters and dollar signs to separate the pieces when needed.

sections.title: General Encoding Requirements and Principles
sections.content:
The RFC establishes three key requirements for all encoding rules. First, encoded values must be octet strings, suitable for transmission in LDAP protocol messages. Second, encoded values should be human-readable and displayable with little or no translation by LDAP client software—this means avoiding binary encoding or escape sequences where possible. Third, encoding rules must be complete and unambiguous, allowing a decoder to recover the original value reliably.

These principles ensure that LDAP can be a practical, human-friendly protocol for directory access. An administrator or user can read an LDAP output and understand what the values mean without decoding tricks. At the same time, LDAP remains formally precise and machine-interpretable. The RFC documents all encoding rules for the standard X.500 attribute syntaxes, and future RFCs can define encoding rules for new syntaxes by following the same principles and format.
sections.eli5: Every attribute type gets a rule that says: write this information as text, make sure it is readable, and make sure the rule is clear enough that you can always decode it back to the original.
